```{r setup}
#| include: false
source("R/tidy_modal_split.R")
library(ggplot2)

RAW <- "data/raw/tran_hv_psmod.json"

frame <- read_jsonstat(RAW)
verify_decoding(frame, RAW)   # stops the render if the index arithmetic is wrong
modal <- modal_split(frame)

# One palette, used the same way in every figure: cars are the series the
# report is about, so they stay the strongest colour throughout and the other
# two modes stay muted. Changing colour between charts would imply the series
# changed meaning.
MODE_COLOURS <- c(
  "Passenger cars" = "#4C7CAE",
  "Trains" = "#4E9A92",
  "Motor coaches, buses and trolley buses" = "#A99CD6"
)

theme_report <- function() {
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
    theme(
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
      plot.title.position = "plot",
      plot.caption = element_text(colour = "grey40", hjust = 0),
      legend.position = "top",
      legend.title = element_blank()
    )
}

EUROSTAT_CAPTION <- paste0(
  "Source: Eurostat, Modal split of inland passenger transport (tran_hv_psmod). ",
  "Data as published ", substr(attr(frame, "updated"), 1, 10), "."
)
```

## What this is

A worked example of reading an official statistical API in R and reporting what
it says, with every number in the prose computed from the data rather than typed
in.

The dataset is Eurostat's **modal split of inland passenger transport**: for each
country and year, the share of inland passenger-kilometres travelled by
passenger car, by train, and by motor coach, bus or trolley bus. The three
shares sum to 100% by construction, so this measures *how* people travel rather
than *how much*.

The raw response is committed at `data/raw/tran_hv_psmod.json` with its SHA-256
and retrieval date in `data/raw/PROVENANCE.md`, so the report renders offline
and the figures cannot drift from the numbers underneath them.

```{r coverage}
#| echo: false
countries <- modal[!modal$is_aggregate, ]
n_countries <- length(unique(countries$geo))
year_range <- range(modal$year)
```

The snapshot covers **`r n_countries` countries** and the years
**`r year_range[1]` to `r year_range[2]`**, though coverage is uneven: not every
country reports every year, and the series are sparse rather than rectangular.

## How complete is the data?

Worth establishing before drawing any trend, because a line chart over a sparse
series invites the reader to interpolate through years nobody measured.

```{r completeness}
#| fig-cap: "Reporting completeness by year. Each cell is one country-year for passenger cars."
cars <- countries[countries$vehicle == "CAR", ]

# as.data.frame(table(...)) makes `year` a factor whatever stringsAsFactors
# says, and as.integer() on a factor returns the level index rather than the
# label. Going via as.character() is what keeps these actual years.
per_year <- as.data.frame(table(year = cars$year), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
per_year$year <- as.integer(as.character(per_year$year))
names(per_year)[2] <- "n_countries"

ggplot(per_year, aes(x = year, y = n_countries)) +
  geom_col(fill = MODE_COLOURS[["Passenger cars"]], width = 0.7) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1990, 2025, 5)) +
  labs(
    title = "Countries reporting a car share, by year",
    subtitle = "Coverage thins out at both ends of the series",
    x = NULL, y = "Countries reporting",
    caption = EUROSTAT_CAPTION
  ) +
  theme_report()
```

```{r best-year}
#| echo: false
best <- per_year[which.max(per_year$n_countries), ]
latest_full <- max(per_year$year[per_year$n_countries >= 0.9 * max(per_year$n_countries)])
```

Coverage peaks at **`r best$n_countries` countries in `r best$year`**. The most
recent year with at least 90% of that peak is **`r latest_full`**, which is the
year used below wherever a single-year comparison is made. Picking the latest
year present instead would compare a handful of early reporters against each
other.

## The long-run picture

```{r eu-trend}
#| fig-cap: "EU-level modal split over time, using the EU27_2020 aggregate."
eu <- modal[modal$geo == "EU27_2020", ]

ggplot(eu, aes(x = year, y = value, colour = vehicle_label)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(size = 1.4) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = MODE_COLOURS) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 100), labels = function(x) paste0(x, "%")) +
  labs(
    title = "The car's share of EU inland passenger travel has barely moved",
    subtitle = "Share of inland passenger-kilometres, EU27 (2020 definition)",
    x = NULL, y = NULL,
    caption = EUROSTAT_CAPTION
  ) +
  theme_report()
```

```{r eu-numbers}
#| echo: false
eu_car <- eu[eu$vehicle == "CAR", ]
eu_car <- eu_car[order(eu_car$year), ]
first_car <- eu_car[1, ]
last_car <- eu_car[nrow(eu_car), ]
car_change <- last_car$value - first_car$value
```

The car share stood at **`r sprintf("%.1f%%", first_car$value)`** in
`r first_car$year` and **`r sprintf("%.1f%%", last_car$value)`** in
`r last_car$year`, a change of **`r sprintf("%+.1f percentage points", car_change)`**
across `r last_car$year - first_car$year` years. Whatever has changed in European
transport policy over that period, it has not changed what share of distance is
driven.

## Who depends on cars most?

```{r ranking}
#| fig-cap: "Car share by country in the reference year, highest first."
ref <- cars[cars$year == latest_full, ]
ref <- ref[order(ref$value), ]
ref$geo_label <- factor(ref$geo_label, levels = ref$geo_label)

ggplot(ref, aes(x = value, y = geo_label)) +
  geom_col(
    aes(fill = geo == "DE"),
    width = 0.7, show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("TRUE" = "#7A6BA8", "FALSE" = "#9DB8D2")) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = sprintf("%.1f", value)),
    hjust = -0.15, size = 3, colour = "grey30"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    limits = c(0, 100), labels = function(x) paste0(x, "%"), expand = c(0, 0)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = paste0("Share of passenger-kilometres travelled by car, ", latest_full),
    subtitle = "Germany highlighted",
    x = NULL, y = NULL,
    caption = EUROSTAT_CAPTION
  ) +
  theme_report() +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(), panel.grid.major.x = element_line())
```

```{r ranking-numbers}
#| echo: false
ranked <- ref[order(-ref$value), ]
top <- ranked[1, ]
bottom <- ranked[nrow(ranked), ]
de <- ranked[ranked$geo == "DE", ]
de_rank <- which(ranked$geo == "DE")
spread <- top$value - bottom$value
```

In `r latest_full` the range runs from **`r sprintf("%.1f%%", top$value)`
(`r top$geo_label`)** down to **`r sprintf("%.1f%%", bottom$value)`
(`r bottom$geo_label`)**, a spread of
**`r sprintf("%.1f percentage points", spread)`**. Germany sits at
**`r sprintf("%.1f%%", de$value)`**, ranking **`r de_rank` of `r nrow(ranked)`**.

## Where rail actually gained

```{r rail-change}
#| fig-cap: "Change in rail share between each country's first and last reported year."
trains <- countries[countries$vehicle == "TRN", ]

# Each country's own first and last reported year, not a fixed window. A fixed
# window would drop every country whose series starts late, which is most of
# the 2004 and 2007 accession states.
change <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(trains, trains$geo), function(g) {
  g <- g[order(g$year), ]
  if (nrow(g) < 2) return(NULL)
  data.frame(
    geo = g$geo[1],
    geo_label = g$geo_label[1],
    from_year = g$year[1],
    to_year = g$year[nrow(g)],
    change = g$value[nrow(g)] - g$value[1],
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
}))

change <- change[order(change$change), ]
change$geo_label <- factor(change$geo_label, levels = change$geo_label)

ggplot(change, aes(x = change, y = geo_label, fill = change > 0)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("TRUE" = "#4E9A92", "FALSE" = "#C9A8A8")) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey30", linewidth = 0.4) +
  labs(
    title = "Change in rail's share of passenger travel",
    subtitle = "Each country between its own first and last reported year, so the windows differ",
    x = "Percentage point change", y = NULL,
    caption = EUROSTAT_CAPTION
  ) +
  theme_report() +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(), panel.grid.major.x = element_line())
```

```{r rail-numbers}
#| echo: false
gained <- sum(change$change > 0)
lost <- sum(change$change < 0)
biggest <- change[which.max(change$change), ]
```

**`r gained` of `r nrow(change)` countries** increased rail's share and
**`r lost`** reduced it. The largest gain is **`r biggest$geo_label`**, up
**`r sprintf("%.1f percentage points", biggest$change)`** between
`r biggest$from_year` and `r biggest$to_year`.

Each bar covers a different span of years, which is stated on the chart rather
than hidden: a country reporting only since 2010 is not comparable with one
reporting since 1990, and forcing a common window would have discarded most of
the newer member states entirely.

## What this does not show

- **Shares, not volumes.** A falling car share is consistent with more driving,
  if rail grew faster. Nothing here measures total distance travelled.
- **Inland transport only.** Air and sea are excluded by the dataset's own
  definition, so this is not a complete picture of how people travel between
  countries.
- **Unequal windows.** Countries enter the series at different dates. Every
  comparison above either uses a single stated year or labels the span it
  covers.
- **No causal claim.** The report describes what the series contains. It does
  not attribute any change to any policy.
